extracted.intended_audience: scholars, editors, and advanced students of textual criticism and classical philology (editing Aristotle and other ancient Greek texts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and practical criteria for establishing manuscript relationships, assessing variant readings, and producing a critical text of Aristotle's Poetics (and similar ancient works). Emphasises internal/external evidence, probability reasoning, palaeography, and use of versions/translations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convincing internal evidence for ancestry
rubrics_metrics.description: Convincing internal evidence would be the occurrence in all MSS. of defects traceable to A only, e.g. the loss of words caused by rents in its material or blots on its pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for the same physical-type defects (omissions, blanks) across witnesses that can be plausibly traced to a single archetype. Example: shared blanks or identical losses that reflect material damage in A. Absence of such common defects weakens the claim that other MSS descend from A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convincing external evidence for ancestry
rubrics_metrics.description: Convincing external evidence would be the statement of a good authority to the effect that A was the first MS. of the book brought to Western Europe, and statements of other good authorities connecting the other MSS. with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek documentary/testimonial evidence (catalogues, ownership records, contemporary reports) linking manuscripts to a known ancestor. Example: a trustworthy note that a particular codex was bought from the loot of Constantinople. Lack of such testimony requires reliance on probabilities instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use probabilistic reasoning when explicit evidence lacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no direct internal or external evidence is adduced, one must consider the probabilities (e.g. owners, historical events, likely dispersal) to evaluate descent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess historically plausible scenarios (ownership, known movements after events like the fall of Constantinople) and dates of copies to infer likely transmission paths. Example: if A's owner perished in 1282 and other MSS appear only after 1453, consider dispersal patterns and purchase histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological plausibility of derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: If all other MSS. are copies of A, they or their ancestors must have been made in Constantinople before the fall of the city, or in Latin Europe after its fall. Hence we should expect the earliest dated MS., which was made in 1457, ... to be derived directly from A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dates of extant manuscripts to test hypotheses about direct descent; if insufficient time exists for recensions to develop between known dates, that constrains possible relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify direct-copy relationships via matching errors/omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: The cases in which we can declare existing MSS. to be copies of other existing MSS. without any hesitation are rare; the most certain case is that of D and d; the Dresdensis appears to be a copy of C, yet if so, some other MS. must have been used with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for near-identical sequences of omissions, the same marginal insertions, or identical corruptions that indicate direct copying. Example: D and d sharing the same omissions gives high confidence of copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared improbable corruptions indicate kinship
rubrics_metrics.description: We notice, then, that D and Ar. agree in 1460 a 2 in the erroneous reading μὴ γνοίη for μιγνύοι; the nature of the corruption is obvious, yet as it involves three itacisms, it is unlikely to have occurred more than once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When witnesses share a complex, unlikely error (multiple itacisms, rare conflations), treat that as strong evidence of common ancestry rather than independent coincidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement on an unsound reading still shows relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purpose of proving kinship between MSS. it is not necessary that the reading on which they agree should be sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not discard shared corrupt readings just because they are wrong — they are valuable genealogical data. Use them to map relationships even if the reading must later be corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arabic (and other version) agreement as an independence test
rubrics_metrics.description: The test, however, which we propose to apply is the Arabic Version; agreement in any considerable matter with that document on the part of a Greek MS. against A may be regarded as evidence of independence of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat agreement between a Greek manuscript and an independent ancient version (Arabic, Syriac) as evidence that the Greek witness may derive from a different tradition than A. Example: Leid. and D agreeing with Arabic on ἔννοια suggests independence from A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer readings requiring fewer corruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Since ἔννοια is by far the less common word of the two, and three corruptions are required to explain one word from the other, it is more likely that ἔννοιαν was corrupted into ἔνια than conversely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating variant readings, prefer the one that needs the fewest and simplest steps of corruption to produce the other readings. Use the principle of lectio difficilior and minimal conjecture where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cross-textual evidence (author's other works) to judge readings
rubrics_metrics.description: The language, as we learn from the Rhetoric (iii. § 7), should be appropriate to the characters and situations; hence the linguistic tragedy is called the appropriate tragedy... The phrase is unconstruable without the Rhetoric; with the aid of that treatise we can interpret it with certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the author's other treatises (Rhetoric, Politics, Natural History, Ethics) to verify meanings and grammatical constructions. Cross-references can confirm or correct ambiguous readings (e.g., sense of technical terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether omissions are accidental or intentional
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1458 a 18 D and its Venetian copy both omit the word not in the definition of 'the virtue of speech'... It is possible that the negative has been omitted accidentally... Yet it seems no less probable that the negative was omitted intentionally by a Christian scribe, who was shocked at the sentiment that the diction ought not to be humble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a meaningful particle is missing, evaluate both palaeographic accident (ink loss, damage) and ideological/intentional motives for omission. Consider context and wider manuscript tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the competence, habits, and speed of scribes
rubrics_metrics.description: How long does Ruosus allow himself for copying all Aristotle’s works except the Logic... 124 days... The work was therefore absolutely mechanical. Nor did these scribes copy for pleasure, but for money... The profession of scribe was a humble one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in known working practices: rapid, paid copying tends to transmit texts mechanically with few emendations; professional editors are likelier to conjecture. Use colophons, known biographies, and palaeographic dates as indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect influence of printed editions and later corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: The marginal corrections of various MSS., e.g. Ambr. 052 and Vat. 1400, seem clearly to be the work of readers who consulted the Aldine edition... Many of the worst are retained by BEKKER; some bad ones even by Curist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for marginal readings and corrections consistent with known printed editions (Aldine, Bekker). Distinguish original hand readings from later marginalia influenced by printed texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat conjectures by editors with caution but record influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Lascaris’s emendations constitute an important epoch... Lascaris conjectured with great boldness; whereas some of his conjectures were afterwards deleted in consequence of better knowledge, others were introduced into the Aldine edition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record conjectural emendations introduced by significant editors; evaluate them against manuscript evidence and later scholarship. Recognise that conjectures can propagate into manuscript margins and later editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Palaeographic knowledge informs likely corruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between oxcoton and oimevon is clearly a case of that corruption of x into te of which Coser has given interesting examples; Athenaeus mistook σκύφος for σίσυφος... confusion of x with ic and of ε with 9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use knowledge of scribal letter-shapes and common graphical confusions to explain specific corruptions. Map likely misreadings (letter transpositions, strokes mistaken) to reconstruct the archetype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use versional glossaries and transliteration patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: The Arabic here has 'in a litter.' This probably represents the word xdivy, which according to the glossaries was used in Syriac, and is merely a transposition of the consonants of LinkE... Since B transposes Avyxez to γλυκεῖ, the transposition of LINKE to KLINE in the Syriac is not surprising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult glossaries and known rendering practices when using versions (Arabic, Syriac) to trace transliteration errors or consonant transpositions that help explain manuscript variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group MSS. by characteristic readings, not solely by provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mimesis Group... The reading after which this group may be named is found in 1459 Ὁ 37, where A Ὁ E exhibit... but BC μέμησις, which agrees with the Arabic simulatio, and is generally agreed to be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish manuscript groups based on shared characteristic readings (naming groups after distinctive variants), and corroborate with independent evidence; provenance alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware easy interpolations (lists, glosses) as later additions
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1458 a 15, after the observation that five neuters end in U, a list of the five is given in Ambr. B 78, Coisl. 34, and the Aldine edition... Of course such a list would be easy to add...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of easily added material (lists, explanatory glosses) appearing in some witnesses and printed editions; test whether such additions are plausibly original or later expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruct readings using internal sense and larger doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: The true reading is then given by E, only for ἤδη we must substitute εἴδει and for ἀνδρείαν ἀνδρεῖον. The construction is 'it is possible for the character to be courageous—and therefore virtuous in agreement with Rule 1—but for the courage to be unsuitable to a woman in species.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When variant readings differ in sense, reconstruct based on coherent interpretation within the passage and consistency with the author's doctrine elsewhere. Prefer readings that make the passage intelligible and consistent with the author's systematic views.
